summary: The rule flags unnecessary Boolean casts (!! or Boolean()) in contexts where values are automatically coerced to Boolean.
fixDescription: Removes the double negation (!!) or Boolean() call, keeping only the inner expression.
hazards: Rewriting !!foo to foo in a comma operator like (console.log(i), !!i < 10) changes evaluation order if foo has side effects, as the inner expression may no longer be evaluated.
Replacing Boolean(!!bar) with !!bar in a context like new Boolean(!!bar) alters behavior because new Boolean() creates an object wrapper, while !!bar is a primitive boolean.
Removing !! from !!foo in foo && !!bar ? baz : bat could change type coercion in the ternary branches if !!bar was ensuring a boolean for consistent comparison.

Stripping Boolean() from Boolean(bar ?? baz) in a logical expression may alter truthiness evaluation if bar or baz are objects with custom valueOf/toString methods that affect coercion differently than direct boolean conversion.

Deleting !! from !!expr in a return statement like return !!expr; is safe only if the function expects a boolean; removing it could return a truthy/falsy value instead of strict true/false, breaking strict equality checks elsewhere.

Removing !! from !!foo in a loop condition like for (; !!foo; ) may cause infinite loops if foo is an object that becomes false only after double negation due to [[ToBoolean]] quirks (though rare, theoretically possible with exotic objects).

Eliminating Boolean() from Boolean((bar, baz, !!bat)) in a comma operator could drop the side effect of evaluating !!bat if bat is undefined and the rewrite leads to parsing errors or unexpected values.

Applying the fix inside nested expressions like if ((!!foo || bar) && !!baz) when enforceForInnerExpressions is true may remove necessary casts if the outer context doesn't coerce to boolean, but the inner !! was for value consistency, not just final coercion.
